A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PASTA research despite the changed title. Their main text, appendices A–G, equations, tables, and figures are sufficiently complete and readable for reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original user-model evaluations, human judgments of PASTA in Figure 5, and simulated-user results in Appendix F.1.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds human-sequence prediction evaluations, final-turn human comparisons, and a Flux transfer experiment.

M1.justification: The overall PASTA pipeline remains intact, but Appendix D.3 adds a CLIP-embedding regularization term to the stated user-model objective. Appendix E.1 changes token-level training from summing individual squared errors to squaring an error based on averaged prefix values. These are localized but substantive optimization revisions; the PDFs do not establish whether earlier experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: v2 adds an explicit transfer scenario: PASTA trained with SDXL is evaluated with Flux.1 without retraining, exposing it to a different image-generation environment. The existing preference datasets and human/simulated interaction coverage remain. Newly disclosed dataset counts do not establish expanded data collection.

E2.justification: The corresponding experiments retain Gemini 1.5 Flash, random prompt selection, and the human-only, simulated-only, and mixed-data PASTA variants. The new final-turn and Flux comparisons also use Gemini 1.5 Flash. Newly cited related methods are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends evaluation design with direct final-turn human comparisons, model-scored human rollouts using the most likely user type, and held-out choice/cross-turn accuracy evaluations. Flux transfer explicitly excludes retraining. Table 2 also changes reported fine-tuning weight decay from 1e-4 to 1e-2; this setting revision alone does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v2 extends user-type sensitivity analysis to human choice and cross-turn prediction accuracy in Figure 4, adds a comparison between model-score trajectories and human-rating trends in Figure 7, and tests robustness to SDXL-to-Flux transfer. These address additional simulator-validity and generalization questions. Existing training-data ablations, simulated reward comparisons, and abstract-prompt examples remain.

E5.justification: Both versions retain 99% confidence intervals for turn-by-turn human judgments and the same uncertainty entries in Appendix F.1. No new seed counts, repeated-run disclosures, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are specified. Additional shaded plots follow the existing practice; the new final-turn percentages have no reported intervals.

E6.justification: v2 adds approximately 70% human choice/cross-turn prediction accuracy, real-rollout score trajectories, and reported relative improvements of 85% in the new final-turn comparison and 20% in Flux transfer. These are additional results under added evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1. The original human-rating plot and Appendix F.1 numerical table are unchanged. Section 6.2 changes the stated performance plateau from 64 to around 16 user types.

T1.justification: The expectile-loss definition is corrected from a weighted x to a weighted x squared. Appendix E.1 also revises the derivation to average token/slate values before squaring, introducing explicit 1/L and 1/Tp factors and changing the expectile term. These are non-equivalent mathematical revisions. The latent-MDP definitions, preference assumptions, and identifiability proposition remain substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: The four central contributions remain. However, v1's introduction claims improvements in both user satisfaction and image quality, whereas v2's corresponding contribution claims improvement in user satisfaction only. The title and terminology changes otherwise preserve the research objective.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new score trajectories as validating correspondence between the simulator and real users, and Flux transfer as evidence of applicability across T2I models. It removes v1's argument that benefits from single-turn training suggest stationary user utilities. The specific rater-bias, demographic, and critique-related limitations in Appendix B.3 remain.

D1.justification: v2 discloses over 7,000 human sequences and about 100 raters, ReLU activations, the two-layer bounded temperature network, kappa4=0.1, and tau_max=3. Conversely, it omits v1's Pick-a-Pic split/tie rules, HPS posterior-conditioning and ranking procedure, and explicit K=8 setting for subsequent experiments. These are localized reproducibility additions and omissions; dataset access remains unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 7 adds a distinction between PASTA's model-agnostic prompt adaptation and methods modifying diffusion noise, attention, or prompt embeddings. Tang et al. (2023) and Salehi et al. (2025), including VIPER, are newly cited, while Moon's EM reference is removed. Most research positioning and cited work remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title and PASTA expansion to preference-adaptive terminology, condenses Sections 5.2–5.3 into a training overview referring to the existing Appendix D, shortens Section 6.2, and merges Section 3.3 into Section 3.2. A generic impact statement is added. Most prose and the overall narrative sequence remain.

P2.justification: The main text switches to a two-column conference layout. The combined architecture figure is split, the user-model evaluation expands from two to four panels, and a new score plot appears. The full three-user-type love illustration moves to Appendix F.2 while a two-type version remains in the main text. These substantially reorganize the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful validation through direct final-output comparisons, transfer across image generators, and prediction tests on human sequences. It also corrects the expectile formula and clarifies implementation details. The gains are limited by missing sample counts, uncertainty, and precise metric definitions for the 85% and 20% summaries, alongside the removal of earlier evaluation instructions. Overall, the evidence supports a limited net quality improvement.
